mcqs.question: Why does every ISA expose only a small number of architectural registers instead of thousands?
options: Registers are simply an arbitrary software convention with no hardware cost
Compilers can only track a fixed small number of values at once
More registers require more wiring to the ALU and a bigger register file, which slows down single-cycle access
Instruction encodings have no limit on register field size
mcqs.explanation: Register file speed depends on staying small and simply wired; scaling it up trades away the single-cycle access that makes registers valuable. Compilers can track arbitrarily many values (spilling extras to memory), and encoding field width very much limits how many registers can be named.

mcqs.question: Why can't a compiler simply repurpose the program counter (PC) to hold a loop counter variable?
options: The PC only exists in RISC ISAs, not CISC ones
The PC is actually just a regular general-purpose register with no special role
Loop counters are always stored in memory, never in registers
The PC is a special-purpose register the hardware itself reads and writes every cycle to track instruction fetch
mcqs.explanation: The PC has a hardware-defined job — pointing to the next instruction — that the fetch stage depends on every cycle. It's genuinely special-purpose (not general-purpose), loop counters are commonly kept in registers for speed, and every ISA, RISC or CISC, has a program counter.

mcqs.question: What's a real cost of an ISA choosing more architectural registers (e.g., 32 instead of 16)?
options: It requires more bits per instruction to encode each register operand
It makes arithmetic operations produce incorrect results
It has no downside at all — more registers is strictly better
It prevents the CPU from being pipelined
mcqs.explanation: Naming more registers requires wider register-number fields in every instruction that references one, competing with opcode and immediate space. It doesn't affect arithmetic correctness or pipelining, and there is a genuine encoding-space trade-off, not a free lunch.

mcqs.question: An x86-64 ISA defines 16 general-purpose architectural registers. Does that mean the physical chip only has 16 register storage locations?
options: Yes, architectural and physical register counts are always identical
No — modern out-of-order chips have many more physical registers and use renaming to map architectural names onto them
No, but only because x86-64 is a CISC ISA; RISC chips always match architectural and physical counts exactly
Yes, because register renaming only applies to floating-point registers
mcqs.explanation: Register renaming maps a small architectural register set onto a much larger physical register file to remove false dependencies — an out-of-order microarchitecture technique. This applies broadly across both RISC and CISC out-of-order designs, and renaming covers general-purpose registers too, not just floating-point.

mcqs.question: Two instructions both write architectural register r1 but compute values with no real data dependency between them. What does register renaming do about it?
options: It forces the two instructions to execute strictly in program order, since they share a register name
It maps each write to a different physical register, so the two instructions no longer share a real destination and the false write-after-write hazard disappears
It deletes one of the two writes, keeping only the last one
It merges both writes into a single combined instruction
mcqs.explanation: Renaming's entire purpose is removing false hazards caused by reusing an architectural name — each write gets its own physical register, so the two instructions are free to execute out of order or in parallel, with later reads wired to the correct physical source. It doesn't force in-order execution (that's the problem being solved), doesn't discard either write, and doesn't merge instructions.

mcqs.question: Why don't ISA designers simply maximize the number of architectural registers to reduce memory spilling as much as possible?
options: More architectural registers widen every instruction's register-naming fields (competing with immediate/opcode space) and increase the state that must be saved and restored on every context switch and call
Hardware is physically incapable of implementing more than 32 registers
Compilers cannot generate correct code for ISAs with more than 32 registers
More registers would make instruction decode literally impossible
mcqs.explanation: The real trade-off is encoding-bit budget (more registers need wider register fields in every instruction) plus ongoing save/restore cost on every context switch and callee-saved boundary — not a hardware ceiling, a compiler limitation, or a decode impossibility. Chips could physically implement far larger register files; the cost is paid elsewhere in the system.
